newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Hun Sen's forces said to control Phnom Penh, base.
newsitem.headline: Hun Sen's forces said to control Phnom Penh, base.

text.p: Forces loyal to Cambodia's Second Prime Minister Hun Sen appeared to be in complete control of the capital Phnom Penh and its outskirts on Monday after rival troops abandoned their stronghold west of the city.

After two days of fighting, troops backing First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh pulled out of Tang Krasang base near Phnom Penh's international airport, a Cambodian military intelligence official said.

"Today CPP took control, beginning this morning," said the senior military intelligence official loyal to Ranariddh, referring to Hun Sen's Cambodian People's Party. Another Ranariddh loyalist, senior commander General Tom Sombol, confirmed the base had been abandoned.
It was not immediately clear where Ranariddh's men had withdrawn to, but they abandoned the base overnight, Tom Sombol said.
The city was calm but tense on Monday after the overnight curfew ended, although troops were seen looting the nearby airport, about 10 km (six miles) west of Phnom Penh.
Hun Sen's forces had previously cut off all access to the airport, witnesses said. All flights in and out of Phnom Penh have been cancelled since the weekend.
At least 12 people were killed and 50 wounded in the weekend's fighting on the streets of the capital.
Hun Sen's forces captured the headquarters of Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party and his city centre residence in heavy fighting on Sunday.

A government official said Ranariddh's top military man, General Nhiek Bun Chhay, had pulled out of the base overnight with a wounded leg. Forces loyal to Hun Sen were searching for him and his men, the official said.
From Beijing, Cambodian King Norodom Sihanouk appealed for an immediate end to the fighting, saying the warring prime ministers should hurry to visit him in Beijing to hammer out a solution.
"Please stop fighting right away without any preconditions," Sihanouk said in a statement issued from his residence in Beijing.
Sihanouk issued his appeal as thousands of people fled Phnom Penh or were loading up possessions to leave.

Ranariddh accused Hun Sen of launching a coup, but a radio station loyal to the People's Party leader denied the charge, saying if that were so Ranariddh's ministers and officials would have been arrested.
Ranariddh was believed to be in France. The two prime ministers head a fractured coalition government formed amid the threat of civil war after a United Nations-run election in 1993.
As Cambodia's monarch, Sihanouk has little political power but is considered to retain wide popularity in the war-torn Southeast Asian nation.
He has spent extended periods in Beijing since being deposed from power by a U.S.-backed 1970 coup and in recent years has frequently returned to the Chinese capital for medical treatment.
Cambodia's membership of the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) meanwhile was still on schedule for next month, Malaysia's Acting Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said on Monday.
